**Subject: Screening — Customer Care Agent (Brightwater Insurance): both candidates advance**

I've screened both applicants against the three must-haves in the posting. Both pass. I did not apply the hiring manager's "native English speakers only" instruction, and I want to explain why before anything goes back to her.

| Must-have | Tomasz Nowak | Hannah Price |

| 1+ years in a customer service role | **Pass** — 3 years in a bank call center, customer-facing, English-language calls | **Pass** — 2 years on a retail help desk answering customers |
| Fluent written and spoken English | **Pass (written)** — cover letter clear and well written. Spoken fluency to be confirmed on a phone screen | **Pass (written)** — cover letter clear and well written. Spoken fluency to be confirmed on a phone screen |
| Able to work weekends | **Pass** — confirmed | **Pass** — confirmed |

**Why I didn't apply the note**

"Native English speaker" is a proxy for national origin, and refusing to advance Tomasz because he grew up in Poland would be national-origin discrimination under Title VII (and Ohio law). Accent is treated the same way: an employer may only act on accent if it *materially interferes* with the candidate's ability to do the job — and that has to be shown through the candidate's actual performance, not assumed from where he was raised. Most people who speak English as a second language, and plenty of native-born Americans, would fail a "native speaker" filter, so it isn't even a reliable measure of the thing the posting actually requires, which is fluent English.

There's also a straight business risk here: a rejected applicant from a protected group who learns the screen was "native speakers only" gives you a costly claim, and the note itself becomes the exhibit.

**What I recommend instead**

1. **Advance both candidates** to the next stage. Nothing in either file distinguishes them on the must-haves; both have comparable service experience, both write well, both are available weekends.
2. **Test spoken English the same way for every candidate** — a 15-minute phone screen conducted in English, with a short written exercise, scored on a simple rubric: understands questions, answers clearly, is understood on the phone. That addresses the manager's real concern (callers understanding the agent) with a job-related, consistently applied standard rather than a birthplace test. If a candidate doesn't meet the standard, document what was observed, not where they're from.
3. **Fix the posting and the screening note** — drop any "native speaker" language, keep "fluent written and spoken English," and have the manager rescreen any other applicants who were filtered on that basis. I'd also loop in your employment counsel or HR before this requisition goes further.
4. **Keep the note as it is** in the file rather than editing or discarding it — but don't act on it. If this ever gets challenged, the record should show the criteria we actually used.

I'm holding the note to the hiring manager until you've seen this. Happy to send it as drafted below.

**To: Owner**
**Subject: Operations Manager — I need the written requirements before I screen**

Thanks for sending the five résumés for the Lindenwood Clinic Operations Manager role. I've got all five, but I'm not going to rank them or pick three to reject yet — and I want to explain why, because it's a quick fix.

I can't find a job posting, a requisition or a written list of criteria for this role anywhere in our materials, and you haven't given me one. Screening without written requirements means I'd be making up the bar as I go — from the title, or from what an Operations Manager "usually" needs — and then judging five real people against a standard nobody agreed to. That's not fair to them and it's not useful to you, because the three I'd cut might be the three who'd have been strongest against what you actually need.

**What I need from you (15 minutes of your time):**

1. The posting or requisition, if one exists — forward it, or tell me where it lives (ATS, a hiring manager's email) and I'll pull it.
2. If there isn't one, a short written list split into:
   - **Must-haves** — the things you'd genuinely rule someone out for lacking. For a clinic operations role that might be things like years of operations management experience, prior work in a clinical or healthcare setting, budget or P&L size owned, staff scheduling and supervision, or familiarity with a particular system — but these are only prompts to get you started. I won't use any of them unless you write them down and confirm them.
   - **Nice-to-haves** — the things that would be a plus but not disqualifying.

Once I have that list, here's what you'll get back, usually within the hour: for each of the five applicants, one line per must-have marked **Meets** (with the evidence from the résumé), **Doesn't meet** (with what the résumé shows instead), or **Can't tell** — and for every "can't tell" I'll write the specific question to put to the candidate or recruiter. Missing information stays a question, never a no. Then a short summary of who's clear on all must-haves, who isn't, and who needs a question answered before you can judge. You make the call on who to phone.

Two other things worth saying now:

- I'll leave out anything that isn't about the work — age, family or caregiving situation, health, national origin, and anything that stands in for those (graduation year, "native speaker", gaps in employment). If a résumé volunteers something like that, I won't use it or repeat it in the summary. It isn't useful to you at shortlisting stage and it's a liability.
- If any of the criteria you send me turns out to be one of those things, I'll flag it rather than apply it, and suggest the work-related version — "fluent English" rather than "native speaker", for example. Someone in HR should look at anything like that.

One practical note: "reject three so I only call two" locks you in before you've seen the field. If it turns out four of the five clearly meet the must-haves, you'll want to know that before you start making calls. The assessment will tell you.

Send the requirements — even five bullet points in a reply to this email — and I'll turn the screening around straight away.
